text: Recently, some studies (e.g., Kossowsky et al., 2012 ) tracked the anxiety disorders of children and adolescents and showed that SAD was persistent and patients deteriorated steadily. Moreover, Lipsitz et al. (1994) suggested that early separation anxiety may constitute a non-specific vulnerability to a wide range of anxiety disorders in adulthood, including panic disorder. Some separation anxiety is a normal part of development in children aged 1–3 years. The lifetime prevalence is between 4 and 7.6% ( Kessler et al., 2005 ; Shear et al., 2006 ; Merikangas et al., 2010 ; Milrod et al., 2014 ), and Manicavasaga et al. (1997) suggest that it may be possible to identify adults whose SAD mirrors the constellation of symptoms observed in childhood, even though some of the specific features are modified by maturation. Therefore, the early detection and intervention treatment of separation anxiety among children and adolescents are vital.
source_label: Development of a Computerized Adaptive Test for Separation Anxiety Disorder Among Adolescents
